qs.q: Which demographic factor is linked to an earlier onset and more symptomatic uterine fibroids?
qs.e: Population studies show higher prevalence and earlier, more severe disease in women of Black African ancestry. The other factors have not been associated with fibroid severity.

qs.q: A 28‑year‑old woman at 12 weeks gestation develops acute pelvic pain and has a known uterine fibroid. Which complication is most likely?
qs.e: Red (carneous) degeneration is common in pregnancy due to rapid fibroid growth and hormonal changes. The other complications are less typical in early pregnancy.

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman is concerned that her multiple uterine fibroids might undergo malignant transformation into a sarcoma. Based on pathologic principles, how often do benign leiomyomas transform into leiomyosarcomas?
o: They transform in approximately 10% of postmenopausal cases
They transform only when associated with multiple chromosomal 6 and 12 rearrangements
They almost never transform into sarcomas
They transform frequently if they develop a parasitic blood supply
qs.e: Leiomyomas almost never transform into sarcomas, and having multiple lesions does not increase the risk of malignancy. Leiomyosarcomas arise de novo from mesenchymal cells rather than from pre-existing fibroids.

es.q: List and briefly describe the main anatomical types of uterine fibroids.
es.m:
-   **Submucosal:** Project into or distort the endometrial cavity; even small lesions can cause heavy menstrual bleeding, infertility, or pregnancy loss.
-   **Intramural:** Arise within the myometrium; large lesions may enlarge the uterus and cause heavy bleeding, pressure, or pain.
-   **Subserosal:** Project outward from the uterine surface; may cause pressure symptoms and abdominal/pelvic mass effect.
-   **Pedunculated:** Attached by a stalk, either submucosal or subserosal; torsion of a subserosal type can cause acute pain.
-   **Cervical or broad-ligament fibroids:** Less common; may distort pelvic anatomy or compress the urinary tract.

es.q: Outline the key epidemiological and risk factors associated with the development of uterine fibroids.
es.m:
-   Increasing reproductive age before menopause.
-   Family history and genetic susceptibility.
-   Black African ancestry, associated with higher prevalence and often earlier or more symptomatic disease.
-   Early menarche and prolonged reproductive exposure.
-   Nulliparity or fewer pregnancies (in some studies).
-   Obesity and metabolic factors.
-   Oestrogen and progesterone signalling support growth, with fibroids commonly shrinking after menopause.

es.q: Describe the initial laboratory and imaging investigations recommended for a patient with suspected uterine fibroids.
es.m:
-   **Full blood count (FBC):** To assess for anaemia and platelet count.
-   **Ferritin:** To confirm iron deficiency, even before severe anaemia develops.
-   **Pregnancy test:** For reproductive-age patients with abnormal bleeding or pelvic pain.
-   **Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal and/or transabdominal):** First-line investigation to describe uterine size, number, location, cavity distortion, endometrium, and adnexa.

es.q: A 40-year-old nulliparous woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, and increasing abdominal girth. Outline the comprehensive approach to her history, examination, and initial investigations to diagnose uterine fibroids and exclude other pathologies.
es.m:
-   **History:**
    -   **Menstrual pattern:** Cycle length, duration, flooding, clots, pad/tampon frequency, night-time changes, and impact on daily life.
    -   **Symptoms of anaemia:** Fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, palpitations, dizziness, and pallor.
    -   **Pressure symptoms:** Urinary frequency, urgency, retention, constipation, rectal pressure, backache, and abdominal enlargement.
    -   **Pain:** Onset, site, severity, relation to menstruation, and any acute changes.
    -   **Fertility intentions:** Duration of trying to conceive, previous pregnancies, and complications.
    -   **Previous history:** Imaging, fibroid treatment, operations, and response.

ai.title: Uterine Fibroids
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Benign smooth‑muscle tumours of the myometrium that cause heavy bleeding, pain and pressure symptoms. Diagnosis is clinical and ultrasound; management ranges from watchful waiting to surgery or medical therapy.

sections.p: Uterine fibroids are benign monoclonal tumours of myometrial smooth muscle, often driven by estrogen and progesterone. They are usually diagnosed by pelvic examination and trans‑abdominal or trans‑vaginal ultrasound.
b: Common in women 30–40 years; prevalence up to 70% in African women

t.b: Is the uterus enlarged and are there focal masses? A normal uterus is <10 cm; any focal mass >1 cm suggests a fibroid.
Provides better detail of submucosal or intramural fibroids; detects size, number and location.
Used when ultrasound is inconclusive or for pre‑operative planning; shows fibroid composition and relation to cavity.

sections.p: The FIGO system classifies fibroids by location and size, guiding treatment choice.

t.b: Determines whether a fibroid is likely to cause bleeding (I–II) or pressure symptoms (III–IV).

sections.p: Hormonal sensitivity, genetic mutations (MED12), and environmental factors are primary drivers. In low‑resource settings, infections and herbal remedies may influence growth.
b: Use of herbal medicines containing phytoestrogens

sections.p: Symptoms depend on size and location: heavy menstrual bleeding, dysmenorrhoea, pelvic pressure, infertility, and rarely pain from degeneration.
Investigations confirm size, number, and impact on the cavity.

t.b: Assesses for anemia due to heavy bleeding; normal Hb >12 g/dL in women.
Low ferritin (<12 µg/L) indicates iron deficiency anaemia.
Detects fibroid size, number and location.
If abnormal bleeding persists >6 months or post‑menopausal, rule out hyperplasia or cancer.

sections.p: Urgent care is needed for severe anaemia, acute pain from torsion or degeneration, or suspicion of malignancy.
Treat the underlying cause, provide symptom control and consider definitive therapy based on size, location and patient desire for fertility.
b: Use of herbal remedies should be discouraged

sections.p: Regular review of symptoms and repeat ultrasound if growth is suspected. Prevention focuses on modifiable risk factors such as obesity and high estrogen exposure.
Differential includes adenomyosis, endometrial polyps, ovarian cysts and uterine sarcoma.
b: Uterine sarcoma – rapid growth and systemic symptoms

sections.p: Ultrasound may miss small submucosal fibroids; normal Hb can mask chronic bleeding.
b: Anaemia may be mild if iron stores are adequate

exam: A 32‑year‑old woman presents with heavy bleeding for 3 months. What is the first investigation? — Pelvic ultrasound to assess size and location of fibroids.
A 45‑year‑old woman with a 10 cm intramural fibroid desires fertility. What is the preferred treatment? — Myomectomy to preserve the uterus.
A patient has a rapidly enlarging pelvic mass and anaemia. What red flag should prompt urgent referral? — Hb <8 g/dL and sudden pain indicating possible torsion or degeneration.
Why is a GnRH agonist avoided in a woman with a history of osteoporosis? — It causes bone loss by inducing hypoestrogenism.
A woman with a submucosal fibroid has normal endometrial sampling. What is the next step? — Repeat trans‑vaginal ultrasound to confirm fibroid location.
What complication is most likely if a pedunculated fibroid undergoes torsion? — Acute pelvic pain and possible haemoperitoneum.
